title: Arrays of deterministic single-photon sources above the loss threshold

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a manufacturable array of emitters that produces single photons on demand and delivers them into one photonic circuit. The emitters would operate together, with sufficiently low loss and sufficiently similar photon properties that photons from different emitters can interfere reliably. The advance is the combination of reproducible fabrication, simultaneous operation and high optical performance across many sources.

Three properties must be distinguished. Single-photon purity describes suppression of unwanted multiple-photon emission, commonly characterized by g⁽²⁾(0), with smaller values indicating stronger suppression. Indistinguishability describes how well photons interfere when their origins cannot be distinguished. Efficiency describes the probability of delivering a useful photon across a specified boundary. An emitter can perform well on one measure while falling short on the others; a low g⁽²⁾(0), for example, does not establish high efficiency or high indistinguishability.

The title's loss threshold refers to a particular loss-tolerant measurement-based linear-optical computing proposal discussed by Ding and colleagues: the product of source efficiency and detection efficiency must exceed two-thirds. This is an architecture-specific condition, rather than a universal threshold for photonic computing or quantum repeaters. A source efficiency above two-thirds alone does not establish that the complete detection chain satisfies it.

Scope synthesis: reproducibly manufactured cryogenic arrays constitute the central breakthrough. Operating an equally capable array at room temperature is an additional accessibility goal. Ambient operation would have to preserve the array's efficiency, photon purity and mutual indistinguishability to satisfy that expanded scope.

significance.text: If reproducible fabrication and simultaneous operation can preserve these properties, the direct consequence would be a manufacturable supply of compatible quantum photons. This would address a source-scaling bottleneck in photonic quantum information processing and support larger experiments involving photon interference, photonic cluster states and quantum communication. The revolutionary step would be making high-performance photon generation available as an integrated component across many emitters.

Fault-tolerant photonic processors and quantum repeaters are conditional downstream possibilities. They would still require suitable architectures, control, sufficiently low circuit losses and effective detection; repeaters would also require the other functions of their networking architecture. Meeting a source target therefore enables system development without demonstrating error-corrected algorithms or a functioning quantum network.

Room-temperature emission could remove the need to cool the emitters, reducing one practical burden of deployment. It would not automatically eliminate system cooling: the documented room-temperature nanotube experiment used superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors. Source temperature and detector temperature are separate engineering constraints.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is replication of exceptional single-source performance across a fabricated array whose emitters work together. The demonstrated quantum-dot approach uses a tunable open microcavity with spatial and spectral adjustment to maximize coupling to a selected emitter. A scalable implementation must preserve strong emitter–cavity coupling and efficient collection without requiring a separately aligned open cavity for every source.

Array engineering synthesis: the challenge includes controlling emitter-to-emitter variation, matching photon frequencies and temporal properties, routing photons into a common circuit, and maintaining performance during parallel addressing. Demonstrating interference between successive photons from one emitter does not establish mutual indistinguishability across many independently fabricated emitters. Fabrication yield and simultaneous performance must therefore be demonstrated alongside the best individual-device measurements.

Coherence must persist across the delays required by the intended circuit, including microsecond-scale delays where relevant. In the retained quantum-dot preprint, corrected indistinguishability decreases from 0.9856(13) at 13.1 ns to about 0.959 at 2.67 microseconds. Its cavity design is also sensitive to displacement: a hypothetical 1 nm cavity-length drift would reduce the maximum Purcell factor by 78%. This quantifies sensitivity, rather than showing that such drift occurred. Single-device stability has been demonstrated, while stability across an integrated array remains unestablished in the supplied reports.

Loss accounting is a separate barrier. Efficient generation and collection must survive coupling, routing and detection losses within the chosen architecture's budget. The documented quantum-dot source efficiency exceeds two-thirds, but its measured source–detector efficiency does not. Scaling must therefore address useful photon delivery throughout the intended chain, rather than relying on an emitter-level efficiency figure.

Room-temperature solid-state emitters face an additional coherence barrier. The nanotube study documents strong ambient-temperature dephasing and reports partial two-photon interference with corrected visibilities substantially below the cryogenic quantum-dot result. The supplied h-BN and GaN reports establish room-temperature single-photon emission but do not establish the near-0.98 indistinguishability proposed here. These studies identify concrete limitations of the documented platforms without establishing a field-wide ranking of all room-temperature emitters.

current_state.text: Ding, Guo, Xu, Liu and colleagues reported a single quantum dot coupled to a tunable open microcavity in Nature Photonics on 28 February 2025. They reported source system efficiency 0.712(18), g⁽²⁾(0) = 0.0205(6), corrected indistinguishability 0.9856(13), and consecutive 40-photon events at 1.67 mHz. These events were sequential detections from one source, not operation of a 40-emitter array. The supplied review had access to the journal abstract through a subscription preview, supplemented by a full preprint and journal supplementary information.

The retained preprint specifies operation at 4 K in a closed-cycle cryostat. Its source-efficiency figure excludes detector inefficiency: the superconducting nanowire detector efficiency was 0.79(2), and the separately reported measured source–detector efficiency was 0.5652(7). Thus the source itself exceeded two-thirds efficiency, while the demonstrated detection chain remained below the cited source–detector product condition. The reported raw Hong–Ou–Mandel interference visibility was 0.928(1); the corrected indistinguishability estimate was 0.9856(13) at 13.1 ns and about 0.959 at 2.67 microseconds. The short-delay corrected value should not be treated as either raw visibility or microsecond-delay performance.

The journal supplement reports six hours of single-device operation without realignment, monitored in 10 s bins, with mean source efficiency 71.1% and standard deviation 0.1%. This is positive evidence of stability under the reported conditions. It does not establish the stability, yield or simultaneous operation of a fabricated array. The supplied review identifies the accessible PDF as supplementary information; it does not substitute for access to the full journal main paper.

Husel, Trapp, Högele and colleagues reported room-temperature telecom photons from nanotube defects in a fiber microcavity in Nature Communications on 11 May 2024. Their corrected Hong–Ou–Mandel visibilities were 0.51 ± 0.21 and 0.65 ± 0.24, with corresponding g⁽²⁾(0) values of 0.31 ± 0.09 and 0.09 ± 0.07. These are reported interference results with substantial uncertainties. The supplied review confirms that the numerical values appear in both the retained preprint HTML and journal PDF text, superseding the earlier limitation to preprint-only verification. Earlier peer-review concerns about sparse coincidence statistics were followed by additional data and analysis and a favorable final assessment; that history does not constitute an unresolved competing experimental result or independent replication.

Chatterjee, Biswas, Fuhr, Aharonovich, Huang and colleagues reported carbon-doped hexagonal boron nitride films in Science Advances on 20 June 2025. A selected emitter operated at room temperature with g⁽²⁾(0) = 0.015 ± 0.002 without background correction and a fitted saturation count rate of 4.66 × 10⁵ counts per second. The count rate is a brightness measurement, not a source-efficiency measurement, and the selected emitter's purity is not evidence of uniform performance across the film. The retained main text does not report two-photon indistinguishability; supplementary figure contents were not supplied for this assessment.

Lecaron and colleagues reported an all-fiber gallium nitride source in Optics Express on 11 August 2025. The retained PubMed abstract describes room-temperature emission at 1292 nm with g⁽²⁾(0) = (5.9 ± 0.5) × 10⁻². It contains no Hong–Ou–Mandel result. The full paper was not captured in the supplied record, so absence of an interference measurement from the abstract cannot establish its absence from the full article.

Evidence-bounded synthesis: none of the supplied reports demonstrates the proposed integrated array combining simultaneous operation, high source-to-circuit efficiency and mutual indistinguishability near 0.98. The room-temperature reports likewise do not demonstrate that combined capability. The supplied freshness record is empty, so these dated results cannot establish whether the combination remained undemonstrated across the field on 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: tens to hundreds of chip-integrated emitters should operate simultaneously and feed one photonic circuit. Suggested per-emitter targets are source-to-circuit efficiency above two-thirds, g⁽²⁾(0) around 0.02 or lower, and pairwise indistinguishability above about 0.98. The purity and indistinguishability targets are motivated by the documented single-source result; the array size and the combined acceptance criteria are proposals, not established standards. Efficiency at the circuit input must be measured explicitly rather than assumed equivalent to the fiber-output boundary of the existing source.
completion_criteria.label: Tens to hundreds of simultaneous emitters meet circuit-input optical targets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed loss-budget demonstration: report source, coupling, circuit and detector efficiencies with their measurement boundaries and uncertainties, and show that the intended architecture's applicable loss condition is met. For the cited loss-tolerant proposal, source efficiency above two-thirds is insufficient by itself; the relevant source–detector product must exceed two-thirds, with intervening losses accounted for consistently. Other architectures should be evaluated against their own requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Full loss budget meets the intended architecture's applicable loss condition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interference demonstration: specify the photon-pair selection, emission delays, filtering and correction procedures. Report raw Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility alongside corrected indistinguishability, and test photons from different emitters during simultaneous array operation. If microsecond-scale delays are part of the intended circuit, performance must be demonstrated at those delays rather than inferred from nanosecond-separated photons.
completion_criteria.label: Simultaneous cross-emitter interference reports raw visibility at intended delays

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical-boundary criteria: demonstrate performance across multiple fabrication batches and independently operated devices, disclose the fraction of fabricated emitters meeting the targets, and report tuning effort, calibration, uptime and drift during sustained parallel operation. A convincing result should show that yield and maintenance remain workable as emitter count grows. These finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within specified operating conditions, not literal universality across all devices, delays or environments.
completion_criteria.label: Cross-batch yield and maintenance remain workable as emitter count grows

completion_criteria.text: Proposed additional room-temperature criterion: repeat the array-level demonstration at a stated ambient operating temperature while retaining the efficiency, purity and interference targets. Disclose any cooling still required for detectors or other components. A cryogenic array can complete the manufacturing scope; ambient emission that misses the array's optical targets would not complete the additional room-temperature scope.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Ambient-temperature arrays retain optical targets with component cooling disclosed

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison synthesis: OPT-01, Cascadable few-photon optical transistor, overlaps through operation with very small numbers of photons and demanding optical coupling. OPT-02 supplies compatible single photons; OPT-01 concerns one optical signal controlling another with sufficient performance for cascading. Source manufacture and transistor gain or cascadability remain distinct capabilities.

Roster comparison synthesis: OPT-03, Room-temperature, electrically pumped laser grown in a silicon CMOS flow, shares the goal of reproducible light-source integration and potentially ambient operation. A laser's electrically driven coherent emission is distinct from on-demand single-photon emission with suppressed multiphoton probability. OPT-04, Laboratory-scale coherent hard X-ray source, also concerns source engineering, but its defining wavelength and coherent-output scope differ from the quantum-photon array proposed here.

Roster comparison synthesis: OPT-05, Video-rate cellular imaging through living tissue, and OPT-06, Practical visible far-field super-resolution optic, concern imaging capabilities rather than manufacture of mutually indistinguishable single-photon sources. Shared optical components or possible future use of quantum illumination would not make either imaging result a demonstration of OPT-02, nor would a source array alone establish either imaging capability.

Roster comparison synthesis: OPT-07, Macroscopic programmable visible optical aperture, overlaps in controlling many optical elements and maintaining coordinated operation. Its defining capability is programmable control of an aperture, rather than high-purity photon generation. OPT-08, The quantum vacuum as a laboratory nonlinear optical medium, concerns access to a nonlinear optical interaction of the vacuum; its quantum character does not make it equivalent to an emitter–cavity manufacturing breakthrough.

Roster comparison synthesis: OPT-09, Few-femtojoule optical links inside computing packages, shares integration, coupling and loss-management concerns, but its defining target is communication energy within computing packages. That target does not itself require mutually indistinguishable single photons. OPT-10, Room-temperature short-wave-infrared photon-counting cameras, concerns detection rather than generation. Such detectors could be complementary where wavelength and performance requirements match, but the roster title does not establish that they meet OPT-02's detector-efficiency or interference-measurement needs.

Historical-overlap limitation: the research notes refer to a historical item 3 as equivalent to this source concept with an added room-temperature requirement. That item's text is absent, so the equivalence cannot be established. It should not be identified with roster entry OPT-03 merely because both use the number 3; the supplied OPT-03 concerns a CMOS-compatible electrically pumped laser.

change_log.reason: The proposed advance is coherent without requiring ambient operation, and no supplied report demonstrates the combined array capability.

change_log.change: Replaced a universal one-third-loss claim with the architecture-specific source–detector efficiency product condition above two-thirds.
change_log.reason: The retained preprint attributes this condition to a particular loss-tolerant linear-optical computing proposal.

change_log.change: Corrected the interpretation of the quantum-dot efficiency result by distinguishing source efficiency 0.712(18) from measured source–detector efficiency 0.5652(7).
change_log.reason: The source figure excludes detector inefficiency; the demonstrated detection chain did not exceed two-thirds.

change_log.change: Added raw interference visibility, correction status and delay dependence to the quantum-dot performance account.
change_log.reason: The corrected 0.9856(13) value applies at 13.1 ns; raw visibility was 0.928(1), and corrected indistinguishability was about 0.959 at 2.67 microseconds.

change_log.change: Integrated demonstrated six-hour single-device stability and qualified the hypothetical cavity-drift calculation.
change_log.reason: The supplement establishes stability under specified conditions, while the 1 nm drift calculation describes sensitivity rather than an observed disturbance.

change_log.change: Clarified that 40-photon events were consecutive detections from one source.
change_log.reason: The reported result does not demonstrate a simultaneous 40-emitter array.

change_log.change: Updated nanotube evidence provenance to include journal PDF text and retained the reported uncertainties and resolved peer-review context.
change_log.reason: The supplied review corroborates the preprint values in the journal text; earlier statistical concerns do not constitute an unresolved contradictory result.

change_log.change: Refined the h-BN result to a selected emitter, uncorrected g⁽²⁾(0), and fitted saturation brightness of 4.66 × 10⁵ counts per second.
change_log.reason: Brightness is not efficiency, and selected-emitter performance does not establish uniform film-level yield or indistinguishability.

change_log.change: Bounded the GaN account to the retained abstract and preserved the missing-full-text limitation.
change_log.reason: Absence of a HOM result in the abstract cannot establish its absence from the full article.

change_log.change: Qualified downstream impact and room-temperature accessibility claims.
change_log.reason: Source arrays alone do not complete processors or repeaters, and ambient emitters do not necessarily eliminate cooled detectors.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to define efficiency boundaries, interference protocols, simultaneous operation, reproducibility and practical operating limits.
change_log.reason: Single-device headline metrics do not establish manufacturable array performance; the proposed thresholds are not official standards.

change_log.change: Added distinctions for all supplied roster entries and retained the historical-item uncertainty.
change_log.reason: Related concepts should remain separate, and the absent historical item's identity cannot be inferred from its numbering.

unresolved_issues: No freshness search record was supplied, so the field-wide state on 1 November 2026 remains unresolved.
The historical item 3 referenced in the research was not supplied; its claimed equivalence to OPT-02 cannot be confirmed.
The GaN full article was not captured, leaving its full measurement scope, including any HOM characterization, unresolved.

The quantum-dot journal main paper was available only as a subscription preview in the supplied review. Detailed interpretation relies on the retained preprint and complete supplement; inconsistent preprint rendering date labels prevent using that rendering to assign journal publication dates.
A separate quantum-dot supplementary PDF had almost no extractable text. Its contents provide no additional basis for conclusions here.
The supplied h-BN supplementary figure contents were unavailable, and the retained main text does not establish two-photon indistinguishability or uniform array-level performance.

The proposed array's architecture, exact efficiency boundary, required emission delays and acceptance protocol must be specified before the numerical completion targets can serve as a definitive experimental test.
Manufacturing yield, mutual indistinguishability across emitters and sustained simultaneous array stability are not established by the supplied single-source reports.

brief.title: Reliable banks of sources for single particles of light
possible: Researchers could feed a light-based quantum circuit with photons, individual particles of light, on demand from many sources working together. Those photons would arrive with little loss and match closely enough to interfere reliably, combining their quantum behaviour.
why: Quantum computing and communication researchers need compatible photons in growing numbers. A reproducibly manufactured component could make larger experiments possible without assembling and adjusting each light source separately.

sources.showed: A cooled semiconductor light source delivered photons efficiently, rarely emitted unwanted extra photons, and produced successive photons that matched closely in interference tests.
sources.cited_for: A single source can combine efficient photon delivery with strong suppression of extra photons and closely matching photons.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not demonstrate an array, and losses including detection exceeded the cited computing proposal's allowance.

sources.cited_for: Room-temperature sources can produce photons that interfere, while collecting light more efficiently than filtering alone.
sources.not_established: The work did not demonstrate an efficient array whose photons match as closely as the proposed target requires.

sources.cited_for: Grown films can host room-temperature sources that rarely emit unwanted extra photons.

This is an experimental study of a room-temperature gallium nitride single-photon source connected entirely through optical fibre.
sources.cited_for: The work supports room-temperature single-photon generation in a fibre-connected device.
sources.not_established: Single-photon generation alone does not establish efficient arrays whose photons interfere reliably with one another.

sources.showed: A later version of the same work.

shown: Ding and colleagues combined high efficiency, rare extra-photon emission and closely matching successive photons in a cooled source. It also ran without realignment for six hours. That demonstrates sustained operation of an individual source.

Husel and colleagues demonstrated partial photon interference at room temperature. Other room-temperature devices strongly suppress extra photons. These results have yet to come together in a manufactured array feeding a shared circuit.
missing: A fabricated array must preserve efficient delivery, rare extra-photon emission and closely matching photons while its sources operate together.
Photons from different sources must interfere reliably across the delays the circuit needs.
Losses through collection, routing and detection must stay within the chosen computing design's allowance.
Repeated manufacturing must produce enough working sources without tuning and maintenance becoming impractical.

milestones.label: Many simultaneous sources meet shared circuit targets
milestones.explanation: Tens to hundreds of sources on a chip would have to feed a shared light-based circuit while meeting delivery, extra-photon suppression and photon-matching targets. This would establish the combined array capability.

milestones.label: The complete photon path meets its loss allowance
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to account for losses from generation through detection and satisfy the chosen computing design's condition. This would establish that enough useful photons survive the complete path.

milestones.label: Different sources interfere at the required delays
milestones.explanation: Simultaneous sources would have to produce interference at the intended delays, reporting both directly measured and corrected results. This would test whether their photons remain compatible in the circuit.

milestones.label: Manufacturing and upkeep remain workable as arrays grow
milestones.explanation: Multiple manufacturing batches and independently operated devices would have to sustain performance, with workable yields, tuning and upkeep. This would establish reproducibility beyond a selected device.

milestones.label: Room-temperature arrays retain the same optical performance
milestones.explanation: An additional demonstration would have to retain the array's optical targets at room temperature and state which other components still need cooling. This would extend the capability beyond cooled sources.

uncertain: The proposed combined array targets are not established standards; the computing design, measurement boundaries and required delays still need definition.
It remains unclear whether room-temperature arrays can preserve both efficient delivery and sufficiently close photon matching.
The cited two-thirds survival condition belongs to a particular computing proposal; other designs have their own requirements.

page.title: Arrays of deterministic solid-state single-photon sources
page.definition: An array of solid-state emitters supplies single photons on demand, ideally one per emitter per trigger. The emitters are semiconductor quantum dots, which are nanostructures with discrete energy levels, or optically active crystal defects. The array couples more than 90% of emitted photons into the optical output and achieves greater than 90% Hong–Ou–Mandel (HOM) visibility between independent emitters without spectral filtering. HOM visibility measures the fractional suppression of coincident detections at the outputs of a beam splitter relative to the distinguishable-photon baseline.

goal.need: Photonic processors need several matching photons in the same clock cycle. With independent probabilistic sources that each succeed with probability p, the chance of getting all n inputs is pⁿ before optical loss. Multiplexing helps, but in one integrated source round-trip loss limited gains beyond 12 time bins. Triggering several emitters together could supply photons for entangling gates with less reliance on multiplexing. Matching photons also serve quantum networks. These uses depend on preserving indistinguishability and limiting losses through routing and detection.

completion.title: A source array exceeds 90% coupling and 90% inter-source HOM visibility without spectral filtering.
completion.criterion: In one array of deterministic solid-state single-photon sources, demonstrate optical coupling above 90% and Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility above 90% between photons from independent emitters within that array, without spectral filtering.
completion.set_by: Members of the Quantum Technologies Virtual Institutes and Virtual Facilities, Quantum Technologies Roadmap (2016), section 2.2.6.F, page 63.
completion.threshold_quote: coupling > 90% and high fidelity (>90% HOM visibility) between independent sources without spectral filtering
completion.basis: The roadmap distinguishes deterministic sources from their replication in arrays. Its coupling target does not establish the source–detector product >2/3 required by Varnava et al.'s loss-focused computing protocol, whose source model excludes multiphoton emission. This is a source-array benchmark, not a demonstration of fault-tolerant computation.

milestones.title: A triggered solid-state emitter produces light with g²(0)<0.5.
milestones.criterion: Under triggered excitation of a single solid-state emitter, measure a normalized second-order intensity autocorrelation g²(0) below 0.5 at zero delay.
milestones.set_by: Single-photon correlation convention, explicitly stated by Chatterjee et al. in Science Advances (2025).
milestones.threshold_quote: value below 0.5 at zero delays indicates single-photon nature.

milestones.title: A source delivers indistinguishable photons with 70% efficiency.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a source of indistinguishable single photons at 70% efficiency using an optimized cavity and excitation scheme. The public deliverable listing leaves the efficiency reference planes and the numerical indistinguishability cutoff unspecified.
milestones.set_by: European Commission Horizon Europe EPIQUE programme, named source demonstrator in its public deliverables listing, updated on 6 July 2026.
milestones.threshold_quote: Fabrication of 70% bright source of indistinguishable single photons based on optimised cavity and excitation scheme

milestones.title: Fabrication yields several dozen identical semiconductor single-photon emitters.
milestones.criterion: Fabricate several dozen semiconductor single-photon emitters and demonstrate optical equivalence across the emitters counted toward that total. The roadmap leaves the numerical tolerance for identity unspecified.
milestones.set_by: QuIC, Strategic Industry Roadmap (2025), page 43; the published fabrication target concerns semiconductor emitters.
milestones.threshold_quote: several dozen identical emitters can be fabricated.

milestones.title: Two independent sources exceed 90% coupling and 90% HOM visibility without spectral filtering.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate optical coupling above 90% for each of two independent deterministic solid-state single-photon sources and Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility above 90% between their photons, without spectral filtering.
milestones.set_by: European Quantum Technologies Roadmap (2016), section 2.2.6.E, page 63; pre-array target.
milestones.threshold_quote: coupling > 90% and high fidelity (>90% HOM visibility) between independent sources without spectral filtering

milestones.title: Triggered photons from at least three independent emitters in one array interfere.
milestones.criterion: In one array, trigger at least three independently addressable solid-state single-photon emitters and use photons from all of them in a common interference experiment. Demonstrate photon correlations that differ from the distinguishable-photon baseline in the manner predicted for quantum interference.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas. No outside body was found to define a separate threshold for this intermediate test.

not_found: The 2016 roadmap does not specify coupling reference planes, visibility corrections, array size, fabrication yield or operating duration.
QuIC's 2025 roadmap does not give a numerical tolerance for identical emitters.
No demonstration meeting the joint array target was found for quantum dots or defect emitters.
The Nature Photonics main text remained subscription-only; its preview and the corresponding arXiv preprint were accessible.
The CORDIS listing for EPIQUE’s 70% source demonstrator is accessible, but its linked report could not be opened.
No roadmap, standards body or programme was found to dispute the value or feasibility of the joint array target.

results.finding: A diamond colour-centre array has 128 channels, with narrow average optical linewidths.
results.detail: The 128 count refers to channels, not necessarily individually characterized emitters. Average linewidths and tuning do not establish optical equivalence across several dozen emitters.
results.quote: We use this process to realize a 128-channel, defect-free array of germanium-vacancy and silicon-vacancy colour centres in an aluminium nitride PIC.

results.finding: Two triggered quantum-dot sources had g²(0) of 1.4% and 2%.
results.detail: The reported uncertainties are ±0.3 and ±0.4 percentage points, respectively.

results.finding: One quantum-dot cavity source had an inferred unpolarized collection probability of 55%.
results.detail: The 55% value is inferred by doubling the measured polarized collection probability; its maximum corrected consecutive-photon indistinguishability was 91.3%.

results.finding: Seventy-five quantum-dot micropillars had a cavity-wavelength distribution with 94 pm FWHM.
results.detail: Cavity wavelength matching alone does not establish emitter equivalence; the quantum-dot wavelength distribution was broader and the interference experiment used two selected sources.

results.finding: Two independent quantum-dot sources achieved 85.3% raw HOM visibility.
results.detail: The authors report no narrow spectral filtering or temporal post-selection. Inferred unpolarized collection probabilities at the micropillar outputs were 55% and 31.2%.
results.quote: Crucially, we perform the experiment without rejecting any useful photons: no narrow spectral filtering or temporal post-selection is used.

results.finding: Five quantum dots produced a zero-delay correlation of 1.52 ± 0.029 in a common-mode interference experiment.
results.detail: The multi-emitter measurements used continuous-wave excitation. Pulsed excitation was demonstrated for HOM interference between two dots, not at least three.
results.quote: Scaling from two to five indistinguishable emitters, we verify interference through cooperative-emission phenomena and Hong–Ou–Mandel two-photon interference, thereby establishing a route towards large-scale, programmable quantum photonic architectures.

definition = "An array of solid-state emitters supplies single photons on demand, ideally one per emitter per trigger. The emitters are semiconductor quantum dots, which are nanostructures with discrete energy levels, or optically active crystal defects. The array couples more than 90% of emitted photons into the optical output and achieves greater than 90% Hong\u2013Ou\u2013Mandel (HOM) visibility between independent emitters without spectral filtering. HOM visibility measures the fractional suppression of coincident detections at the outputs of a beam splitter relative to the distinguishable-photon baseline.". Reason: The definition needs to explain deterministic triggering and optical coupling and identify the baseline for Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility.

goal.need = "Photonic processors need several matching photons in the same clock cycle. With independent probabilistic sources that each succeed with probability p, the chance of getting all n inputs is p\u207f before optical loss. Multiplexing helps, but in one integrated source round-trip loss limited gains beyond 12 time bins. Triggering several emitters together could supply photons for entangling gates with less reliance on multiplexing. Matching photons also serve quantum networks. These uses depend on preserving indistinguishability and limiting losses through routing and detection.". Reason: The current text describes a single-source experiment and leaves the practical bottleneck and the benefit of an array unexplained.

Skipped proposed operation 3 (remove statement 1): the entry needs at least 2 statements. Its reason: The NIST statement describes a goal for an individual on-demand source, and its array refers to holes in that source’s nanocavity.

add statement by European quantum-technologies roadmap community, 2016: "Arrays of deterministic single photon and photon pair sources". Reason: The named-goal section omits the roadmap that expressly sets the array goal.

edit completion: criterion = "In one array of deterministic solid-state single-photon sources, demonstrate optical coupling above 90% and Hong\u2013Ou\u2013Mandel visibility above 90% between photons from independent emitters within that array, without spectral filtering."; set_by = "Members of the Quantum Technologies Virtual Institutes and Virtual Facilities, Quantum Technologies Roadmap (2016), section 2.2.6.F, page 63."; threshold_quote = "coupling > 90% and high fidelity (>90% HOM visibility) between independent sources without spectral filtering"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 27, 3]. Reason: The consultation identifies the roadmap editors, and the criterion can specify that the interfering emitters belong to the array under test.

edit m1: criterion = "Under triggered excitation of a single solid-state emitter, measure a normalized second-order intensity autocorrelation g\u00b2(0) below 0.5 at zero delay."; refs = [7, 28, 29]. Reason: The criterion mixes the correlation threshold with an experimental result and needs to specify that the measurement is taken under triggered excitation.

edit m2: criterion = "Demonstrate a source of indistinguishable single photons at 70% efficiency using an optimized cavity and excitation scheme. The public deliverable listing leaves the efficiency reference planes and the numerical indistinguishability cutoff unspecified."; threshold_quote = "Fabrication of 70% bright source of indistinguishable single photons based on optimised cavity and excitation scheme"; threshold_ref = 8. Reason: The criterion embeds a one-dot result and omits the cavity and excitation conditions in EPIQUE’s public deliverable description.

edit m3: title = "Fabrication yields several dozen identical semiconductor single-photon emitters."; criterion = "Fabricate several dozen semiconductor single-photon emitters and demonstrate optical equivalence across the emitters counted toward that total. The roadmap leaves the numerical tolerance for identity unspecified.". Reason: The criterion embeds a fabrication result and leaves unclear that optical equivalence must be demonstrated across the emitters counted toward QuIC’s target.

edit m4: title = "Two independent sources exceed 90% coupling and 90% HOM visibility without spectral filtering."; criterion = "Demonstrate optical coupling above 90% for each of two independent deterministic solid-state single-photon sources and Hong\u2013Ou\u2013Mandel visibility above 90% between their photons, without spectral filtering."; threshold_quote = "coupling > 90% and high fidelity (>90% HOM visibility) between independent sources without spectral filtering"; threshold_ref = 6. Reason: The threshold quotation omits the independent-source and no-filtering conditions, and the criterion embeds experimental results.
